articles.title: Nuclear fallout to flowerbeds: Japan to reuse Fukushima’s nuclear cleanup soil in flowerbeds and public works before 2045 deadline
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Japan is preparing to take another step in its long-running effort to manage soil removed during the cleanup of areas affected by the 2011 Fukushima n.
articles.body: Japan is preparing to take another step in its long-running effort to manage soil removed during the cleanup of areas affected by the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. The government has decided to begin reusing decontamination soil at government facilities in Sendai, Miyagi Prefecture, and Saitama, marking the first such use outside Tokyo apart from demonstration projects in Fukushima itself. The Environment Ministry plans to use the material in flowerbeds at government buildings in the two cities. The move is part of a broader government policy aimed at reducing the enormous volume of soil currently held at interim storage facilities in Fukushima. Authorities are working towards a legal deadline requiring final disposal outside Fukushima Prefecture by March 2045. The decision also places greater emphasis on demonstrating the proposed reuse of treated soil in locations beyond the disaster-affected region, while addressing public concerns over its safety.How Fukushima cleanup soil will be reused before the 2045 deadlineThe initial projects will involve flowerbeds at government buildings in Sendai and Saitama, according to the government’s decision reported by Japan Today. The programme follows earlier demonstration efforts and a government initiative to establish practical examples of reusing soil generated during Fukushima's extensive decontamination programme. The material was collected after the 2011 earthquake and tsunami triggered the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident and widespread radioactive contamination. Large quantities of removed soil have since been placed in interim storage facilities within Fukushima Prefecture. The government has promoted the reuse of soil containing relatively low concentrations of radioactive substances as part of its longer-term management strategy. Similar reuse has already taken place at government sites in Tokyo, including the Prime Minister's Office. The expansion to Miyagi and Saitama represents a significant geographical step in testing whether the approach can gain acceptance beyond the areas directly associated with the disaster.Government faces 2045 deadline for Fukushima soil disposalThe regional reuse programme is closely tied to Japan's longer-term obligation to remove the decontaminated soil from Fukushima. The government aims to complete final disposal outside the prefecture by March 2045, making the development of reuse schemes an important part of its strategy for dealing with the stored material. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara described the regional projects as an important step towards that objective and called for similar initiatives to be expanded to government branch offices elsewhere in Japan. The scale of the challenge is substantial, with soil generated across years of decontamination work remaining in interim storage. A government roadmap has prioritised reuse, public communication and progress towards eventual off-site disposal. The approach is intended to gradually establish examples that can demonstrate how the material can be managed outside Fukushima while creating greater public understanding of the government's proposed strategy.Safety concerns remain central to Japan's soil reuse planThe decision to move Fukushima decontamination soil into other prefectures also places public acceptance at the centre of the programme. Government officials have repeatedly stressed the importance of communicating scientific information about the material's safety as reuse expands. Kihara urged authorities to strengthen public communication alongside the new regional projects. The government has previously used controlled demonstration sites to show how low-radioactivity soil could be incorporated into landscaping and other applications. Under the broader policy, officials are seeking to establish confidence through visible examples before expanding reuse further. The Japan Atomic Industrial Forum reported that the government's roadmap includes scientific information sharing, site visits and continued monitoring, alongside consultation with Fukushima and other local authorities. The Miyagi and Saitama projects will therefore serve not only as disposal measures but also as tests of how far Japan's controversial soil-reuse policy can be extended.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Aunt who died in Middlesbrough house fire was 'beautiful soul'
articles.summary: Two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder over the fire in Middlesborough, police say.
articles.body:
A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".

Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday.

Cleveland Police said the fire had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.

Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".

She said Valentina, also known as Tina, had been spending the summer holidays with the family.

"She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."

She also said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape through an upstairs window.

The friend, she said, had "kicked out a window" and "had saved their lives".

Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area and encourage anyone who has concerns, or who may have information, to approach our officers."

Patrols had been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said earlier.

articles.title: 160 killed in deadly Nepal deluge; at least 133 Indians among 844 missing
articles.summary: India News: Water rose 30 feet and at least 160 people were killed, while hundreds of others, including scores of Kailash Mansar-ovar pilgrims from India, remaine.
articles.body: Water rose 30 feet and at least 160 people were killed, while hundreds of others, including scores of Kailash Mansar-ovar pilgrims from India, remained missing after a flash flood and mudslide of unprecedented scale in Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers tore through a part of Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday morning. It swept away settlements, hydropower units and the pilgrim route.Nepal Police put the toll at 157, while Chinese authorities reported three deaths and 265 people missing in Tibet’s Gyirong county. Nepal Police said 579 others — 466 foreigners from 28 countries and 113 Nepalis — remained untraced, including at least 133 Indians. Among the missing were at least 37 NRIs. Frighteningly, as many as 33 bodies were found 150km downstream at Chitwan, showing how far the dea-dly waters carried victims.Pilgrims were planning to cross border when flood hitAmong the missing foreigners were 54 Americans, 34 Australians, 33 Britons, 24 Canadians, 19 Malaysians and 8 Koreans.Many were Kailash Mansarovar pilgrims, with nearly 400 of them, including the Indians, preparing to cross the Nepal-Tibet border or travelling through the region when the flood struck.ALSO READ | Nepal floods: MEA issues helpline numbers as over 100 Indians go missingRescue personnel battled poor weather, mud, washed-out roads and high river levels even as authorities moved families from vulnerable settlements to safer locations.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal told parliament that 29 police personnel and 44 soldiers remained untraced after floodwaters swept away their barracks in Rasuwa, while customs officials, hydropower workers and other employees stationed near the border were also missing. At the 20MW Langtang Khola Hydropower Project, dozens of workers are out of contact. The torrent also swept away or inundated security posts, customs facilities, banks and other establishments along the river corridor. Nepal PM Shah appealed for patience and unity as the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force deployed helicopters, drones, boats and ground teams for search-and-rescue operations.Across the border, floods and mudslides severed several roads, communications and electricity around the (dry) Gyirong port, a key Nepal-Tibet crossing used by Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrims. Chinese president Xi Jinping called for “all-out efforts to search and rescue people who are missing”.The flood destroyed critical infrastructure across northern and central Nepal, with preliminary govt estimates showing at least 19 bridges and around 40 km of roads damaged or washed away; 13 hydropower projects were hit, and around 200 trucks were lost. articles.title: Wes Streeting deluged with homophobic hate mail since becoming defence secretary
articles.summary: Homosexuality was decriminalised in the UK in 1967, but a ban continued in the armed forces until 2000.
articles.body:
The Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, has said he faced more online homophobia in the weeks since he was appointed than in his whole life.

Streeting said he had received an "unbelievable volume" of abuse because people "couldn't cope" with the idea of an openly gay person leading the armed forces.

In an interview with the Iain Dale All Talk podcast at the Edinburgh Fringe, he said his new role was an opportunity for him to demonstrate strength and "to challenge the sort of stereotype that clearly persists in dark corners of the internet".

Homosexuality started being decriminalised in the UK in 1967, but a ban continued in the armed forces until 2000.

Speaking on the podcast, Streeting said: "I have experienced more online homophobia in the last three weeks than I have in my entire life.

"An unbelievable volume, because people cannot cope with the idea that a gay person might lead the armed forces of the United Kingdom."

"Being the first openly gay defence secretary has been almost entirely unremarked upon in the media," he added.

"And I think, 'great, here we are in the third decade of the 21st century it doesn't matter, brilliant'. But of course online it matters to a lot of people.

"And I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we've gone from gay people not being able to serve in the military to a gay defence secretary."

However, Streeting said he had also been congratulated by people in the Ministry of Defence for being a symbol of progress.

He said: "In my first week, someone in the MoD said to me: 'As a gay man, I'm really proud that we have our first gay defence secretary - It means a lot to many of us who remember the bad old days.' I was quite touched by that."

articles.title: FaZe Clan: How three teenagers posting Call of Duty trick shots in 2010 built a gaming brand worth over $1 billion
articles.summary: US Streamers News: FaZe Clan did not start with investors, executives, or a billion-dollar valuation. It started on May 30, 2010, when three teenage gamers - Eric “CLipZ.
articles.body: FaZe Clan did not start with investors, executives, or a billion-dollar valuation. It started on May 30, 2010, when three teenage gamers - Eric “CLipZ” Rivera, Jeff “House Cat” Emann, and Ben “Resistance” Christensen, created FaZe Sniping. Their setup was simple: bedrooms, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, and a love for pulling off difficult sniper trick shots. The early content was built around montages and high-skill plays, not business plans. One of the biggest early boosts came from “ILLCAMS,” a synchronized YouTube series that packed their wildest gameplay together. The FaZe name began carrying its own status inside gaming, turning a small online group into a recognizable identity. Then the model changed. Thomas “FaZe Temperrr” Oliveira and Richard “FaZe Banks” Bengtson became key figures in management, helping move the brand beyond anonymous gameplay and into personalities, vlogs, creator houses, and influencer-led content.The Call of Duty group grows into something much biggerThat shift gave FaZe a much bigger lane than Call of Duty alone. The organization pushed into esports and built championship-level teams in Counter-Strike, Call of Duty, Fortnite, and Rainbow Six Siege.It was no longer just a channel for sniper montages; it had become an organization spanning competitive teams and creator personalities. FaZe also connected gaming with streetwear, hip-hop, and traditional sports.Snoop Dogg, Lil Yachty, and NFL player Kyler Murray joined the organization, while partnerships with Nike and Takashi Murakami expanded its image.Nasdaq brought the billion-dollar momentThe real financial test arrived in July 2022. FaZe went public on the Nasdaq through a merger with a Special Purpose Acquisition Company, trading under $FAZE.The market debut came with huge retail-investor excitement, and the company’s valuation briefly moved above $1 billion. For a brand born from teenage gaming clips, that number was massive. But the public-market story quickly turned in the other direction.FaZe struggled with monetization, heavy cash burn, and weaker sponsorship revenue. Within a year, its stock had fallen more than 90% and was trading below $1 per share, making it a “penny stock.” By early 2024, FaZe was no longer an independent public company.GameSquare Holdings, a media company backed by Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, acquired the organization at an equity value of roughly $17 million to $47 million.The deal effectively erased the billion-dollar public-market peak. The gap between those numbers was enormous, especially because the company had recently been valued above $1 billion.FaZe went back toward its internet-first rootsThe brand did not stop there. After the acquisition, GameSquare created FaZe Media as a separate corporate division and returned FaZe Banks to a leadership role as CEO.The business also cut down its bloated operation, removing multiple corporate executives and mainstream creators while refocusing on internet culture, streaming events, and gaming audiences.That makes FaZe’s story less like a clean rise to the top and more like a wild loop: bedroom trick shots, cultural empire, celebrity-backed expansion, Nasdaq hype, collapse, then a return to its internet-first roots in its latest corporate structure.The brand’s latest structure is built around the audience and culture that made its original name matter.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Burnham calls summit of first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
articles.summary: The announcement comes as Burnham holds his first official visit to Wales since becoming prime minster.
articles.body:
The prime minister says he will bring together the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland in the autumn for a summit.

Andy Burnham made the announcement ahead of a visit to south Wales on Thursday - his first official visit to the country since he took control of the UK government.

The Labour leader said he wanted "every leader in this country signed up" to having "good jobs in every community".

Downing Street said the first ministers of Wales and Scotland, and the first and deputy first ministers of Northern Ireland will meet the prime minister at the National Economic Council in October.

Burnham is visiting a location in south Wales as part of his listening tour.

His spokespeople said he will speak to Welsh workers and apprentices about "reindustrialisation, jobs and the cost of living".

Burnham said: "I am in South Wales today because the answers to the UK's challenges will not come from an echo chamber. They will come from the places that know their own strengths, and from a government willing to listen and then act.

"Good jobs in every community, in every part of the UK. That is what I want every leader in this country signed up to."

He will meet the Welsh government's deputy first minister Sioned Williams at the visit.

Williams said the visit was "a positive example of governments working together to improve people's lives".

She will call for a "fair share of the UK government's steel fund", an "energy social tariff to support those facing fuel poverty and struggling with high energy bills", and high standing charges in Wales to be addressed.

She added: "Wales is an energy-rich nation. People should see that reflected in good jobs, stronger communities and lower bills."

The National Economic Council was created by the Gordon Brown administration in 2008, and has been revived by Burnham.

A previous meeting brought together government ministers and English local authority mayors.

Downing Street said the prime minister wanted to discuss "how we will drive good growth in every postcode across the UK" with the first ministers.

The Welsh government said: "We look forward to discussing shared challenges, including ensuring growth and investment in all the countries represented, and support for families facing the continuing cost-of-living crisis.

"This is alongside further discussions with the UK government to progress broader priorities in Wales, including fair funding and extending devolution."

Plaid Cymru has pressed the UK government for discussions over more powers and funding for the Senedd - Wales's parliament - and the Welsh government in Cardiff.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth had his first meeting with the new prime minister on the sidelines of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games in July.

At the time, ap Iorwerth said it was "too early" to know whether the new Labour prime minister would agree to his calls.

Downing Street said then that the prime minister wanted an "open and ongoing dialogue" with the first minister.

articles.title: Neath woman alleged to have mis-sold horses via Facebook
articles.summary: Five women tell the BBC they were mis-sold unsafe and injured horses by a seller on Facebook.
articles.body:
When her teenage daughter was lying motionless on the floor after being kicked in the head by a horse, Fiona feared the worst.

"For a moment, I thought she was dead," she said. "I thought she had broken her neck."

The horse Fiona bought six weeks earlier via Facebook was marketed as a "teenager's dream" but during a riding lesson, it bucked and bolted with her daughter partially on it before kicking her in the head.

Now Fiona, whose name has been changed to protect her daughter's identity, is one of five women who have told the BBC they were mis-sold horses that were either unsafe to ride or had life-limiting conditions by horse seller Tasha Lee Hopkins.

Fiona's 13-year-old daughter was rushed to hospital in an ambulance with concussion and spent about two weeks recovering at home from her injuries after the incident at a riding arena in south Wales.

"You could see on the side of her helmet, the hoofmark where she got kicked in the head," said Fiona.

"I was thinking, 'oh my gosh she's going to be paralysed.' It was just awful."

Fiona witnessed the "terrifying" moment and was "absolutely horrified" to later discover she had been sold a horse that had never been sufficiently trained to ride.

"I trusted Tasha. I believed what she said and she sold us a horse that wasn't fit for purpose, it wasn't fit for a child to be riding," added Fiona.

A leading horse welfare organisation has warned of "too many cases" where horses that cannot be ridden are given away or sold "until they end up in a really poor situation".

World Horse Welfare said unlike other animals such as dogs, there are no regulatory or voluntary industry standards for horse trading, so it is "vital" that sellers and prospective buyers do their due diligence.

Fiona bought the 14-year-old horse from Hopkins in December 2024.

It had been advertised on Facebook group CT Sports Horses, which is run by Hopkins and another person, and describes itself as selling "safe sports horses" that have six-month warranties.

"We went to view the horse and met Tasha and she seemed lovely, it all felt very genuine," said Fiona.

"It wasn't until the horse arrived back at home that it all started to unravel."

After the incident, Fiona tracked down the horse's original owner. They said they had owned the animal since it was two - and during that time the horse had not been ridden.

Fiona claims Hopkins didn't disclose this information when she bought the animal.

The BBC has found this was not the first time Hopkins, from Neath near Swansea, is alleged to have mis-sold a horse in the last seven years.

While five women have claimed they were mis-sold horses by Hopkins, another two have told us they had concerns about her operation.

One buyer alleged she was sold a horse for riding by Hopkins that had an undisclosed broken back.

Another claimed Hopkins sold a horse for showjumping which had such severe arthritis, a vet had previously recommended it should be put down.

That horse, Otto was bought for £6,250 by Kayleigh Sweet in March last year after the 37-year-old saw an advert on Facebook and was told by Hopkins it had recently been checked and cleared by a vet.

"[Hopkins said] he was a 'perfectly sound five-year-old'," recalled Sweet.

But within a week of owning him, Sweet noticed Otto - a warmblood breed that was about 17 hands tall - had gone lame and was struggling to walk.

When she looked at his medical history, she noticed there was "no history, no vaccinations, nothing, and that's really unusual".

She then tracked down Otto's original owner, who told her that as a three-year-old he had been diagnosed with chronic arthritis in his leg.

Sweet said she was told the horse had been operated on but it had not improved enough for riding - and the vet had advised them to put the animal down.

Sweet said the then owner gifted him as a companion horse instead - meaning he would be kept as a pet. But Otto ended up being sold and ultimately owned by Hopkins.

An examination by Sweet's own vet confirmed the diagnosis but when she told Hopkins, she said she refused to honour the six-month warranty.

Otto's arthritis diagnosis was devastating for Sweet, who'd previously had to have another horse put down due to the exact same issue.

"I just had to relive it all over again and it's horrible," added Sweet, from the Vale of Glamorgan.

She took legal action and earlier this month Hopkins appeared at the County Court in Swansea where she was ordered to pay Sweet £11,000 in damages and expenses, which had been due in October 2025.

During the legal proceedings, Otto was returned to Hopkins. Sweet doesn't know what has happened to him since.

Another person, Hayley Vaughan bought a horse called Bonnie for £1,400 from Hopkins for her 16-year-old daughter Amber after seeing an advert on Facebook in 2019.

But the 55-year-old said her daughter only rode her once before they had to call the vet.

"She looked really uncomfortable, we decided to get her x-rayed," recalled Vaughan from Haverfordwest.

Scans showed Bonnie had a serious back injury and a painful spinal condition.

"The vet said there was no way she could ever be ridden," added Vaughan.

After the horse kicked out with both hind legs in the stable - a sign that it was in pain - she said the vet told her "don't you ever let your child ride that horse".

Vaughan contacted Hopkins after the discovery.

"She [said she] would take the horse back but not give me my money back."

"There was no way I was giving that horse back to her. I wish I'd had the courage to take her to court."

Vaughan found Bonnie a retirement home to ensure she could live out her life in the right conditions but says she lost all the money she'd spent on the horse.

The BBC put all of these allegations to Hopkins but she did not respond to our questions.

The BBC also asked Facebook's owner Meta about the CT Sports Horses Facebook group and associated adverts on the site - and it said it has now "removed the content brought to our attention for violating our policies".

The five women who claim they were mis-sold horses by Hopkins told the BBC they viewed the animals but didn't have a pre-purchase examination by a vet.

World Horse Welfare recommends to all prospective buyers to view the horse in person, get it checked by your own vet and ride - if appropriate.

"Just be really vigilant, do your homework, go through the passport," added Sweet.

She is now calling for horse passports to be made digital because some buyers have said the paper format can lead to key information about the horse's medical history being undisclosed during the sale.

"I don't think I'll ever find peace until there's some underpinning security for animals and for people when it comes to processes like this," said Sweet.

"People should have the truth from day dot and things aren't masked, because you can quite easily get a replacement passport for a horse that has nothing in it."

The Welsh government said: "While paper passports remain a legal requirement, we recognise the opportunities digital technologies may offer to strengthen equine identification records."

articles.title: Accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, 3 co-defendants set for 2028 trial
articles.summary: A military judge set a 2028 trial date for accused 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three alleged co-conspirators held at Guantánamo Bay.
articles.body: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, and three alleged co-conspirators will stand trial in 2028, a military judge ruled Wednesday. Lt. Col. Michael Schrama set the trial for June 5, 2028, rejecting prosecutors’ request to begin proceedings in January 2027. Mohammed and the three other defendants have been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003 in the long-delayed case stemming from the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people. Schrama said the prosecution’s proposed Jan. 11, 2027, trial date did not leave enough time to resolve outstanding pretrial matters. "A realistic trial date must account for the hearing and resolution of pretrial evidentiary and compliance motions, including the FBI LHM suppression motions," Schrama wrote. COURT THROWS OUT PLEA DEAL FOR 9/11 MASTERMIND KHALID SHEIKH MOHAMMED, TWO OTHER TERRORISTS The scheduling order establishes a series of deadlines and milestones for the case leading up to the June 2028 trial, while leaving existing deadlines governing ongoing pretrial litigation in place. "The TSO issued today serves as the overarching scaffolding. It assumes the successful completion of the deadlines in the AE 989O TCO and the FBI LHM TCO and establishes milestones leading to a trial on the merits starting on Monday, 5 June 2028," Schrama wrote. Under the order, jury selection, including assembly, challenges and empanelment of commission members, will begin June 5, 2028. Opening statements are scheduled to begin 30 days after the members are empaneled. The defendants may choose to defer their opening statements until prosecutors have finished presenting their case. COURT PUTS PLEA DEAL ON PAUSE FOR 9/11 MASTERMIND KSM: 23 YEARS LATER, JUSTICE FOR TERRORISTS IS DELAYED AGAIN Prosecutors will begin presenting evidence immediately after opening statements conclude. Once the prosecution rests, the defendants will have 14 days to seek a finding of not guilty under the Rules for Military Commissions. The prosecution would then have 14 days to respond to such a motion, followed by seven days for the defendant to reply. If prosecutors choose to reopen their case to address an alleged deficiency raised in the motion, the order gives them 45 days after the conclusion of their initial presentation of evidence to do so. The defendants are scheduled to begin presenting their own evidence 60 days after prosecutors conclude their case-in-chief. The order also sets procedures for rebuttal and surrebuttal evidence, additional motions for findings of not guilty and closing arguments. Schrama wrote that, absent good cause, the commission will not grant extensions or continuances involving motions for findings of not guilty or the presentation of rebuttal or surrebuttal evidence. JUDGE RESTORES CONTROVERSIAL 9/11 TERRORIST PLEA DEALS INVOLVING KHALID SHEIKH MOHAMMED: REPORT The trial date comes after years of legal wrangling over the prosecution of Mohammed and his co-defendants, including a failed effort to resolve the case through plea agreements. A divided federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., ruled in 2025 that then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin had the authority to withdraw from plea agreements that would have allowed Mohammed and two co-defendants to plead guilty in exchange for sentences of life in prison without parole, potentially taking the death penalty off the table. Austin argued that a decision on whether to remove the possibility of capital punishment should rest with the secretary of defense. The D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 that Austin acted within his legal authority when he withdrew the agreements. "Having properly assumed the convening authority, the Secretary determined that the families and the American public deserve the opportunity to see military commission trials carried out," Judges Patricia Millett and Neomi Rao wrote in the majority opinion. "The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment." Mohammed, a Pakistani national, is accused of spearheading the Sept. 11, 2001, plot in which hijackers crashed commercial airliners into the World Trade Center and Pentagon. A fourth hijacked plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in Pennsylvania. The 2028 date sets a timetable for a case that has remained in pretrial proceedings for years as the military commission has addressed disputes over evidence and other legal issues before a trial on the merits can begin. articles.title: Victims of Oregon quintuple homicide include suspect’s girlfriend, her relatives and friends
articles.summary: The victims of what is being investigated as a quintuple homicide at a rural home outside Portland were identified Monday as the suspect’s girlfriend, her mother, her grandmother and two friends, authorities said.
articles.body: FOREST GROVE, Ore. — The victims of what is being investigated as a quintuple homicide at a rural home outside Portland were identified Monday as the suspect’s girlfriend, her mother, her grandmother and two friends, authorities said. The suspect was found dead in his car in Enumclaw, Washington, about 187 miles north from where the bodies were found in Forest Grove, Oregon. Police believe the suspect, 36-year-old Benjamin Charles Parker, killed himself. The Washington County Sheriff’s Office said the victims include Parker’s girlfriend, 26-year-old Stella Jade Kimsey; her 60-year-old mother, Rowan Karla Kimsey; and her 85-year-old grandmother, Mary Elizabeth Kimsey. Stella Kimsey’s best friend, 26-year-old Linsey Mae Haraldsen, and Haraldsen’s partner, Alvin Raymond Chu, 27, were also among the dead. Authorities said Rowan Kimsey owned the property about 30 miles west of Portland and lived there with her daughter, Stella, along with Parker. Two cats and two dogs were also found dead at the scene. Another cat was transported to a vet for treatment but was later euthanized due to the extent of its injuries. The sheriff’s office did not specify how the people and animals died. Authorities found the five bodies on Saturday and announced the homicide investigation on Sunday. They noted the complexity of the investigation and the large crime scene. “I will say that in my 22 years here, I have not been a part of or witnessed a scene quite this complex involving this type of an investigation,” Sheriff Caprice Massey said.

articles.title: Caste count method in Census ‘misleading’: Congress letter to PM
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Terming the methodology for caste count adopted in Census 2027 “misleading” as it will not give a headcount of OBCs, leaders of opposition .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Terming the methodology for caste count adopted in Census 2027 “misleading” as it will not give a headcount of OBCs, leaders of opposition in Parliament, Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, have written to PM Narendra Modi demanding the Census questionnaire on caste notified recently be abandoned and a new one be drafted. They underlined that the word “OBC” has not even been used in the Census.In the backdrop of the controversy triggered by the questionnaire, Kharge and Rahul told the PM “your govt” has adopted an “open-ended question” to collect information about caste, and enumerators will have to take for an answer whatever a person replies to the caste question. They argued that a caste is known by different names and sub-castes depending on the region, which would result in one caste being recorded by thousands of names. “This would result in lakhs of castes being registered in the country, and the entire data recorded in the caste census would become useless,” the letter said.“We don’t approve of the caste census being done through this methodology. Govt should cancel the present questionnaire and prepare a fresh one through consultations with political parties, experts, and the public so that a correct headcount of every caste and community is collected and the caste census is precise, relevant, and beneficial,” it said.It said a readymade solution to the problem is that a “drop-down menu” comprising a list of castes be added to the questionnaire. “This very methodology is used for counting SCs and STs (in Census)... This methodology was adopted in the surveys of Bihar and Telangana. We are enclosing the caste lists of the two surveys for understanding.” Further, the letter said such a list of castes for Census can easily be compiled on the basis of the existing Socially and Educationally Backward Classes list and data from the Anthropological Survey of India.Releasing the letter, AICC spokesperson Jairam Ramesh and OBC department chairperson Anil Jaihind said govt had, in an affidavit to SC in Sept 2021, submitted that a “drop-down menu” with a list of castes will have to be used if a caste census were to be done. articles.title: Tribe accuses US federal agents of ‘trespassing’ on indigenous border land
articles.summary: The Tohono O’odham people have sued the US government to stop construction of a border wall through their reservation.
articles.body:
An Indigenous tribe located between the United States and Mexico has accused US federal agents and construction workers of illegally trespassing on its land to begin work on a controversial border wall in the state of Arizona.

In a statement released on Tuesday, the Tohono O’odham Nation said “approximately 20 masked, armed Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents” accompanied construction workers to three locations before dawn.

The statement added that CBP prevented tribal police from issuing trespassing citations to the contractors.

CBP had cordoned off the area with a “vehicle blockade” and deployed a special weapons and tactics (SWAT) team to protect the contractors, according to Tohono O’odham authorities.

Mexican police had also been deployed to keep watch, the statement said, also noting the presence of a “tethered balloon” for surveillance purposes.

“At this time, interactions between [Tohono O’odham police] and federal law enforcement have been peaceful and professional,” the statement said. “We will continue to monitor the situation.”

The early-morning activity is the latest chapter in a years-long fight between the Tohono O’odham and the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has pushed to build a border wall through the tribal nation’s land.

The conflict stretches back to Trump’s first term in office, from 2017 to 2021, when he proposed a border-spanning barrier to deter irregular migration into the US.

But many Indigenous groups, including the Tohono O’odham, opposed the construction, which threatened to bulldoze sensitive habitats, sacred sites and other parts of tribal land.

A federally recognised tribe of around 37,000 members, the Tohono O’odham Nation sits along roughly 100km (62 miles) of the US-Mexico border. Its territory straddles the US state of Arizona and the Mexican state of Sonora.

The tribe has members in both countries, who often cross without passports or other documentation beyond their tribal identification cards.

Under US law, federally recognised tribes are considered “domestic dependent nations”. They exercise sovereignty over their own land and are not subject to state-level laws.

But their relationship to the US government is particularly fraught. The degree to which federal authorities can impose their will on tribal nations has long been the subject of heated legal battles.

The border wall has been at the centre of some of those fights. In June, the Tohono O’odham legislature voted unanimously to file a lawsuit against the Trump administration over efforts to appropriate tribal land for the barrier.

The nation argued that it had cooperated closely with federal authorities to stop irregular border crossings and drug smuggling, spending millions of dollars on the effort.

It claims that cross-border detentions have dropped by more than 95 percent as a result of that work.

Attempting to trespass on tribal land to build a border wall would be a violation of Indigenous rights, the Tohono O’odham Nation has said. It maintained it had not been asked for consent prior to construction.

By pushing ahead, the Indigenous nation argued that the US Department of Homeland Security “has chosen to disregard our sovereignty, ignoring proven border security strategies and dismissing the irreversible environmental and cultural destruction that will follow”.

“We have been left with no other choice,” the tribal government added. “We would prefer to use the resources that the litigation will require for services directly to Nation members. But our priority MUST always be to protect our people, our culture, and to stand up for what is right.”

On August 14, however, US District Judge Richard Leon declined to issue a preliminary injunction to stop the border wall’s construction on Tohono O’odham land.

Tuesday morning’s construction activity appears to be a result of that decision.

The Trump administration has argued the land along the border does not belong to the tribe. Instead, it has pointed to a 1907 proclamation declaring the area roughly 18 metres (60 feet) around the border as federal land for security purposes.

In 2023, however, a report from the Government Accountability Office, a US federal watchdog agency, found that the border wall effort had caused harm to Indigenous land, including by “blasting at a tribal burial site and altering water flows”.

In recent months, the Tohono O’odham tribe has put up large signs warning against trespassing on its reservation.

articles.title: US judge declines Minnesota’s effort to force Texas to extradite ICE agent
articles.summary: ICE agent Christian Castro faces criminal charges for shooting a Minnesota man in the leg during an immigration raid.
articles.body:
A United States judge has denied a request to compel the extradition of a federal immigration agent charged with shooting a man during an immigration raid in the state of Minnesota and lying about it.

Wednesday’s decision concerns the case of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent Christian Castro, who has been detained in a county jail in Texas since May.

Minnesota has sought his extradition as he faces charges of assault and falsely reporting a crime in Hennepin County, which covers Minneapolis.

Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for more than 90 days. At that point, the suspect must either be transferred or released. The deadline for Castro is set to expire on Thursday.

Minnesota argued in a lawsuit this month that Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican, has refused to authorise the extradition for political reasons.

But in Wednesday’s ruling, Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr wrote that he could not intervene because Abbott has not yet acted – and has therefore not yet violated any law.

“The record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro,” Rodriguez wrote.

Castro has been charged in connection with the non-fatal shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis during an immigration raid in Minnesota on January 14, part of a mass deportation effort under President Donald Trump.

Starting in December, Trump oversaw a large-scale deployment of federal agents to the Midwestern state , dubbed Operation Metro Surge.

The operation, which lasted less than three months, sparked protests and allegations of civil liberty violations from residents and watchdog groups.

Prosecutors say Castro fired a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg.

Afterwards, he and another agent accused Sosa-Celis and another man of assaulting federal authorities with a broom handle and snow shovel. Those allegations were later disproven after video of the incident emerged. Criminal charges against Sosa-Celis were subsequently dropped.

Todd Lyons, then-acting director of ICE, confirmed in February that the agents appeared to have made “untruthful statements”. Castro and the second agent were placed on administrative leave.

Castro is currently in custody in Brownsville, Texas. Minnesota officials have warned that he may flee the country if released, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico.

During those calls, Castro talked “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released”, according to Minnesota’s lawsuit.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week to stop Castro’s anticipated release and force Governor Abbott to sign the extradition warrant.

Ellison has framed Abbott’s decision not to take action as a way of supporting Trump’s mass deportation campaign and skirting federal extradition law.

“For nearly three months, Greg Abbott has refused to return ICE agent Christian Castro to Minnesota, where he’s charged with shooting a Minnesotan in his own home,” Ellison wrote in a social media post.

“Abbott has a legal obligation to return him. Instead, he’s chosen to ignore the law.”

articles.title: Meta's $18bn settlement may hasten reckoning for social media on child safety
articles.summary: Perhaps our days of doomscrolling are numbered, writes the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman.
articles.body:
Meta's decision to settle the case on Wednesday came as a surprise.

I was expecting weeks of courtroom drama as 29 states – almost two-thirds of North America - took on one US tech giant.

Technically, the trial was about children's online privacy. It was based on a US law called the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), which is nearly 30 years old and predates all of today's biggest social platforms.

It centred around Meta's historic gathering and use of data belonging to children under the age of 13 over a period of several years.

In reality, it was a co-ordinated attack on the firm's online safety credentials.

Meta, alongside other social media apps, is under fire around the world as 2026 is shaping up to be a year of reckoning for the entire industry - perhaps our days of doomscrolling are numbered.

Meta to pay up to $18bn to settle claims its platforms harm children

Meta has fought hard, over multiple lawsuits spanning many months and at great expense, to defend its commitment to protecting children on its platforms.

More than once, I've been invited to detailed presentations at Meta's London HQ, where senior executives have walked journalists like me through the many safety tools the company has launched over the years designed to give children better protection on its apps.

I have also met the parents of young people who have come to harm on those same platforms, and others who admit to being totally overwhelmed by the sheer number of safety tools that require their oversight - at the last count Meta had more than 60 of them, and that was just on Instagram.

The trial went on for just five days, and came to an end before CEO Mark Zuckerberg took to the stand.

Whistleblower Arturo Bejar, who once worked at Instagram, claimed that in the past he had told bosses that harmful stuff was happening to children on the platform, and no action was taken.

Another executive said he didn't remember writing on a slide deck that sometimes Meta chose to pay fines for violating regulations rather than make changes.

Internal memos suggested that the firm knew opt-in tools tended to have low adoption rates, and yet it still launched safety features that were not switched on by default.

There had been intense speculation that Meta would have faced hundreds of billions of dollars in fines if it had lost.

The worst-case scenario, which would have been the maximum penalty imposed for every single child who used one of its platforms for more than half an hour a day during a 12-year window, was $1.4tn (£1tn) – roughly the same as the company's entire value.

That of course was never going to happen, but a more realistic figure was still in the hundreds of billions.

By comparison, up to $18bn (over a period of 10 years) is significantly smaller.

Meta is not admitting to any wrongdoing.

You could argue that settling protects its core business - social networks are still the way in which it makes most of its money.

Instagram and Facebook's billions of users provide the company with a goldmine of data, and the data of adults can be used to sell ads.

Meta may say it is now laser-focused on AI, but it still needs the vast revenue generated by its social apps.

As part of the settlement, the social media giant has agreed to make a number of changes to the way Instagram and Facebook operate for its youngest users.

The new safety barriers include a two-hour time limit across both platforms, which will be a default setting for known teen users. But direct messaging on the platforms will not count towards the daily use limit.

Notifications will be muted between midnight and 06:00 and on school days between 08:00 and 15:00.

Likes on posts and content will also be entirely hidden on the platforms for teens.

Most of these new features will be made either default or an option for teens within six months.

However, new efforts by Meta to better identify which users on its platforms are children will take up to a year to be rolled out.

I would be surprised if these measures remain within the confines of the US for very long, as other countries will almost certainly be keen to adopt them too.

Meta also says the new features will only truly help children if all of its rivals adopt them as well.

It's a highly competitive industry, but given the global backlash against social media and its impact on children, perhaps others like TikTok and Snapchat may have to follow suit.

The question then is whether children will still bother with them, once they are deliberately toned down into a much blander offering.

And perhaps that would bring the social media era to a natural end, as existing adults gradually aged out of it.

Arturo Bejar, the ex-Instagram engineer turned whistleblower, says the proof of the pudding will be in whether the new teen safety features are effective.

"At the end of the day, Meta needs to be held accountable for results, not efforts," he told me.

articles.title: Plug-in solar panels are coming to a shop near you - what to know
articles.summary: The UK government claimes panels could help homes "significantly cut" energy bills.
articles.body:
Plug-in solar panels will be hitting the shelves of DIY shops and High Street retailers after the government changed the rules to allow them to be legally sold in the UK.

They are significantly cheaper than roof panels, can be installed without an electrician and are suitable for properties with outdoor space, including some balconies.

Retailers including Argos will be stocking products from Thursday, and the government expects other shops to follow suit.

It hopes plug-in solar panels will help households save money and reduce reliance on overseas fuel sources, the price of which has fluctuated in recent months due to the Middle East conflict.

Customers should get their wiring checked by a professional to ensure it is safe before parting with cash, experts say.

Will plug-in solar panels save me money?

The government hopes the plug-in panels will offer people a more affordable way into solar energy compared to roof installation, although savings will be lower because they generate less power.

A one-panel kit will cost £699 while two-panels will be £1,089, according to UK solar company UKSOL.

The government expects prices to settle at £400-£600 as competition increases and more products are developed.

Its research shows a household could save between £70 and £110 a year on their energy bills.

The precise amount will depend on how the panels are orientated and how long they run. An unshaded south-facing spot is best.

Households which use energy during daylight hours will benefit most as the electricity must be used as it is generated.

Any power not consumed will flow back to the grid, but it's unlikely homes will get any cash for this.

Unlike rooftop solar panels, these systems do not need to be certified under the official Microgeneration Certification Scheme (MCS), which is the UK's official quality mark for small-scale renewable energy systems.

But it also means they will not normally qualify for the Smart Export Guarantee that pays people for excess solar power.

The panels will make a difference to a household's power consumption but it is deliberately modest for safety reasons.

While kits may come with panels that are capable of generating more power, the microinverter - which turns the current from the panel into electricity homes can use - will limit output to the home to 800 watts.

That's enough to cover "always-on" electrical appliances such as fridges and devices left on standby. The government says it should power about a fifth of the average household's electricity use while the sun is shining.

Other essentials, such as the kettle which needs 3 kilowatts of electricity, will be powered through a mix of the 800 watts flowing from the panel with the rest coming from the national grid.

British Gas said plug-in panels won't solely power a home but can "meaningfully reduce how much electricity you need to buy during the daytime".

Government tests found sample systems could operate with no unacceptable heating or unsafe energy flows.

Each device comes with a microinverter which constantly monitors the connection to the grid.

If the electricity cuts out, from a power cut for example, or if the panel is simply unplugged, the microinverter senses that and shuts down in milliseconds so it can never push live electricity into dead wiring.

To be legally sold in Great Britain, new panels must be tested against the industry's G98 standard and the government's product specification.

If a panel meets these requirements, it will appear as compliant on the Energy Networks Association's public register , so it is definitely worth checking before buying.

Consumer safety charity Electrical Safety First said buyers should stick to established retailers and their own websites rather than third-party sellers on online marketplaces.

It warned that some platforms are not currently legally responsible for the safety of goods sold through them.

Are these devices suitable for every home?

Not necessarily, according to Electrical Safety First, which has published a list of steps to help households reduce any risks before buying.

The charity's main worry is that plug-in solar can interact with older safety devices in some home electrical systems.

It recommends having electrics checked by a registered electrician before buying panels, particularly in older properties or where the age and condition of the wiring is unknown.

It also said households should never connect one through an extension lead, cable reel or plug-in adaptor, as these can overheat.

And for now, it advises sticking to a single plug-in device per household.

The panels will come with a mounting kit and instructions. Tools may be needed but professional installation isn't required.

Once mounted, connect the microinverter and plug into a mains socket - ideally a external socket that is weatherproof.

They aren't permanently attached so they can be moved to a different property.

People may need permission from their landlord, freeholder or building owner.

Households will need to let the electricity Distribution Network Operator (DNO) know within 28 days of plugging the panel in. This is the company that owns the cables in the area, not your energy provider.

articles.title: Scottish Highlands benefiting from 'coolcation' trend
articles.summary: Scotland and other northern European nations are seeing more tourists as people avoid the heat.
articles.body:
"People used to come to the Highlands and say, 'it's beautiful – shame about the weather'. Now they're coming for the weather."

James MacLeod, concierge at the Glencoe House Hotel, in the Scottish Highlands, is talking about how he has noticed a big shift in visitors' perceptions.

"They don't seem to care about the midges or the rain anymore," he chuckles. "They're just glad it's not too hot."

Climate change is redrawing Europe's summer tourism map.

Wildfires, droughts and record-breaking heatwaves are making summer months increasingly uncomfortable and unpredictable across southern Europe. By contrast, Scotland and other northern European nations are finding themselves perfectly positioned to offer a "coolcation" escape.

The early data backs this up. Visitor numbers to northern Europe were up 10% across April to June of this year, compared to the same period in 2025, according to the European Travel Commission (ETC), the body that represents Europe's national tourism bodies.

The ETC said that northern Europe, which it classifies as Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Sweden and the UK, had "outperformed all other European subregions".

Meanwhile, travel agency Trip.com found that from January to April of this year searches for cooler holiday destinations this summer had increased by 74% from the first four months of 2025, "as travellers seek to escape the heat, shifting their attention to places that offer more comfortable climates".

And Awaze, the European holiday-rental group, says searches for "escape the heat" rose three-fold in the past three months, while hunts for "coolcation" were up more than four-fold. Within the UK, holiday rental website Cottages.com said that its Scottish portfolio has been the most viewed this summer.

Back in Glencoe, Emily Bryce, operations manager at the National Trust for Scotland, says that visitor numbers this summer are up 8% from a year ago. "Visitors tell us it's refreshingly cool here compared with the south of France and Spain." She laughs: "Today it's drizzle and 13 degrees."

Chris Greenwood, a senior researcher at Glasgow Caledonian University's Moffat Centre for Travel and Tourism Business Development, points to a "massive shift" in where high-net-worth UK families go on their summer holidays. He says that a growing number are swapping the likes of Tuscany for the Scottish Highlands.

Greenwood also points to how Scotland is changing how it promotes itself. "In 2026, Scotland stopped selling itself as 'rugged' and started selling itself as 'temperate'," he says.

How the threat of extreme heat is starting to change our holiday plans

The northward shift of holidaymakers in Europe is not unique to Scotland or the Nordics.

Dutch costal city The Hague recently made headlines after a New York Times article described it as a new "coolcation" hotspot while "southern Europe overheats".

The city combines international institutions and urban culture with 10km (six miles) of coastline, beach bars, dunes and cycle routes stretching along the shore.

But success brings its own risks. Streets in Kijkduin, a popular costal district of The Hague have had to be officially closed to all but residents at times this summer, to prevent gridlock caused by a huge influx of cars with Belgian, German and Dutch numberplates.

Up the coast in the town of Zandvoort residents took matters into their own hands, putting up fake diversion road signs to try to keep tourists away.

Similar overcrowding woes can now be seen in the Scottish Highlands. "It's busier than the carpark at my local mall," says Nick, visiting from the US. He had passed another full layby in Glencoe valley, a particularly picturesque and popular part of the Scottish highlands that attracts large numbers of overseas tourists.

Holidaymakers are grinning and posing before heading to the next beauty spot.

Many of Scotland's other Instagram-famous destinations are also under strain from the volume of tourists, says Greenwood. He describes the Fairy Pools on the Isle of Skye (which are a series of natural pools and waterfalls) and Edinburgh's Royal Mile as becoming "victims of their own virality".

To mitigate the impact of visitor numbers to the Scottish capital, Edinburgh last month became the first city in the UK to introduce a tourist tax. A 5% fee will be added to the cost of hotel room in the city.

It is expected to raise as much as £50 annually. "We know that the city's popularity comes at a cost through the pressure it puts on our services and on the people who live and work here all year round," said Edinburgh Council Leader Jane Meagher.

"This small new contribution from overnight visitors will help improve the services and public spaces we all depend on, while better managing the effects of tourism and major events."

In Glencoe the National Trust for Scotland has expanded parking areas and is investing in a 5km cycle route. There's also a plan to introduce a park-and-ride system, and offer shuttle buses between the mountain ranges.

"There will always be people who want to stop and take a quick selfie," Bryce says. "We need to provide alternatives [to going by car]."

Yet Scotland has not been spared the impact of drier weather this summer. Wildfires scorched both the Highlands' Cairngorms National Park and Edinburgh's Arthur's Seat in July.

And at the other end of the year, the Glencoe Mountain Resort skiing centre is having to adapt to unreliable winter snow. Its chairlift, once mainly for skiers, now carries mountain bikes to the top of a downhill track.

I watch my 10 year old daughter Zena races through heather nearby, building boulder bridges over a cold stream, clinging to my brother as the Etive Mòr and Black Mount mountains rise behind them.

Thirty years ago my father brought us here to ski. We would wait to see red deer that posed outside the local Kingshouse Hotel. The stags weren't there this time. Instead tourists at sunlit picnic tables were photographing themselves.

The real test of this new love for the Scottish wilderness is whether it leaves enough wilderness for the next generation.

articles.title: Who are Alyshia Rushing’s family? Everything to know about Mama A’s husband and four children
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Alyshia “Mama A” Rushing, the TikTok creator who shared her life as a mother with hundreds of thousands of followers, died at 26 after a two-vehicle c.
articles.body: Alyshia “Mama A” Rushing, the TikTok creator who shared her life as a mother with hundreds of thousands of followers, died at 26 after a two-vehicle crash in Montgomery, Alabama, on August 22. She left behind four children: Karter, Raelynn, Zoey and Aydan. A GoFundMe campaign has since been created to support the children and their father, who is now caring for all four. The fundraiser describes the children’s loss as “unimaginable” and says their mother had been their caregiver, provider and “safe place.”Who is Alyshia Rushing’s partner and father of her children?Alyshia Rushing did not publicly share the name of her children’s father. Although family moments appeared on her social media, she kept his identity mostly private.The GoFundMe campaign says he is now the sole caregiver for Karter, Raelynn, Zoey and Aydan. It was set up to help him handle the children’s needs while the family deals with Alyshia’s death. The campaign says donations can help with food, clothing, housing, school expenses, transportation, activities and counseling.Alyshia also spoke about her relationship in one of her final social media updates. She said she had separated from the father of her children and was trying to get her life back on track. That gave followers a glimpse into what she was dealing with personally before her sudden death.There is no reliable public information confirming that Alyshia was married to the father of her children. For that reason, describing him as her husband would go beyond what has been publicly confirmed.Who are Alyshia Rushing’s children Karter, Raelynn, Zoey and Aydan?Alyshia’s four children are Karter, Raelynn, Zoey and Aydan. They were a major part of the content that helped her build a following on TikTok.The GoFundMe campaign says Alyshia was not only their mother but also their caregiver and provider. It says their father is now responsible for caring for all four children and preparing for their needs in the months ahead.The fundraiser was created after her death to provide practical support for the family. It also asks people to help the children as they adjust to life without their mother.Alyshia, who had nearly 540,000 TikTok followers, became known online as “Mama A” through videos about motherhood, family routines and everyday life. She began posting in 2024 and often centered her children in her content. WSFA 12 News also reported that she was a Tuskegee resident and identified her as the creator behind the “Mama-A” TikTok account.Her death came after a crash on Interstate 85 in Montgomery. A preliminary crash report obtained by WSFA said Alyshia and 20-year-old Landon Dunn, who was driving the other vehicle, were killed. A passenger in Alyshia’s vehicle survived with injuries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis: 'If you started running, they shot you'
articles.summary: Many communities are living in fear of being kidnapped for ransom as the crisis spreads further south.
articles.body:
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."

The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.

"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.

It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.

Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."

About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.

She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.

Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.

Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.

Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.

But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.

Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."

She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".

Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.

Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.

Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.

Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.

Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.

"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."

Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.

Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.

When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.

The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.

They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.

Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period last year.

Data from Nigeria's National Human Rights Commission shows that the number of kidnappings across the country doubled over the same period.

Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".

Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.

As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.

Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

'Peace is a gradual thing': How land, cattle and identity fuel a deadly Nigerian conflict

Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.

At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.

But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.

This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.

Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.

After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.

The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.

"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.

"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.

Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.

The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.

A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.

President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.

In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.

But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.

The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".

"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.

One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.

He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.

"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".

"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.

He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.

"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."

He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.

Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.

"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."

She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.

The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.

Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.

"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

articles.title: Jon Stewart asks whether 'The Daily Show' is like high-sugar food giving US 'political diabetes'
articles.summary: Jon Stewart told Michelle Obama he wonders whether "The Daily Show" has been cultural "ultra processed food" giving America political diabetes.
articles.body: Talk show host Jon Stewart told former first lady Michelle Obama Wednesday he questions whether shows like his have been a net positive or net negative for the country. On her "IMO" podcast, Obama asked Stewart whether it’s healthy for young people to get their news from "The Daily Show." "Do you think comedy helps or hurts the political climate?" she asked. "I wonder what you think, because sometimes I think, ‘Is it good that most young people are getting their news from The Daily Show?’ Or that they — you know — they want you to run for president?" Stewart began by questioning his show's impact, saying that late-night shows are becoming a "relic." JIMMY KIMMEL FIRES BACK AT CRITICS TELLING HIM HOW TO DO HIS JOB AS LATE-NIGHT COMEDIAN "We are in some ways a relic of a previous era where it's sort of like I'm running a Blockbuster, a video store inside of a Tower Records," Stewart replied, noting social media’s impact and how even his show has had to adapt to it to boost reach. Multiple commentators have noted that the late-night talk show as an entire format appears to have been increasingly outmoded by long-form podcasts. Stewart went on to note that he has learned not to confuse cultural power with actual power but nonetheless appreciated how cathartic shows like his can be. He said the format feels somewhat "impotent" and possibly like something of an "opiate" for American citizens. "Is it an opiate?" he asked. "Is it creating a, you know ... And having worked on some of those things on Capitol Hill and all that, I know the difference now, which I didn't before. The difference between activists who are in the trenches doing that day-to-day work, trying to bend that arc of the moral universe slowly towards justice, not realizing there's a bunch of people trying to bend it back." COLBERT CALLS TRUMP 'AUTHORITARIAN' BUT REJECTS 'PARTISAN' LABEL IN EXIT INTERVIEW WITH NY TIMES Stewart said he is curious about what a double-blind study would show about his work. "Like, does this help? Does it corrode? Does it pervert? Is it something to be — is it ultra-processed, you know, food that's given the country a kind of political diabetes? I don't know," he said. "I think I also have to step back on — it may not be an honorable thing we do, but we do it as honorably as we can in that it is not in bad faith," Stewart continued. "So, the way that I try and judge it is, any good faith art, material, speech, talk that goes into the universe, I feel like is a win. "There's so much bad faith," he warned. "But I can't sit here and honestly answer like, ‘It's a win for society. What I've done over these past 25 years,’ you know, I'd hate to think, obviously, but there's many people on social media who would tell me, you know, that that is the case." Tim Graham, the executive editor of the NewsBusters division of the Media Research Center, agreed that Stewart is right to question what his show has done for political discourse. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The concept of Americans getting their 'news' from comedy shows is always a terrifying prospect," Graham began. "Stewart's right with his metaphor of ultra-processed food. Political comedy's a Twinkie and not a bran muffin. People can have very distorted views on a comedy-alone diet, like thinking Sarah Palin actually said, ‘I can see Russia from my house.’ "Late-night comedy can be compared to an opiate because their natural audience uses their overwhelming tilt against Trump to get over their anger that Trump won the White House again," he continued. "In 2024, the late-night shows devoted 82% of their political jokes to Trump and the Republicans. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's a little bit funny that they're discussing partisan hackery on the Michelle Obama podcast," Graham added. "The Obamas have been the most fawned-over couple in modern American media history. Late-night comedians never act on the Michelle principle, ‘When they go low, we go high.’"
